newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-German crew heads for Mir space station.
newsitem.headline: Russian-German crew heads for Mir space station.

text.p: The cash-strapped Russian space agency on Monday launched its latest team of cosmonauts into space to take command of the Russian Mir space station, bringing along a German cosmonaut for a three-week visit.
The three cosmonauts blasted off from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan at 5:09 p.m. (1409 GMT) on Monday, space officials said.

"The launch at Baikonur was without any problems," said Valery Lyndin, a spokesman at mission control outside Moscow. "The module with the cosmonauts separated from the booster and the cosmonauts are now in orbit."
"They are beginning preparations for docking," scheduled for February 12, he added shortly after take-off.

German cosmonaut Reinhold Ewald, 40, is due to stay aboard Mir for 20 days before returning to Earth with the current Mir crew, Valery Korzun and Alexander Koleri. The two have been aboard the station for the last six months.

Russians Vasily Tsibliyev, 42, and Alexander Lazutkin, 39, are scheduled to remain in space along with U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger, who began to work at the station on January 15. They are scheduled to return to Earth in June.
Ewald is flying under an agreement between Germany and Russia in which Germany will pay millions of dollars for the ride -- a welcome fillip for the struggling Russian space industry.

Funding problems have delayed several missions in recent months, forcing cosmonauts to stay aboard Mir longer than planned. Russia has nevertheless promised to go ahead with its contribution to the next generation Alpha space station.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union caused severe funding problems for Russia's space programme, foreign financial assistance for joint missions has become a vital source of support.
Germany has said it considers Ewald flight important as preparation to return to the international Alpha space station in the future. Alpha will be assembled in stages starting later this year.

The 120-tonne Mir space station was first launched in 1985, and is expected to be in use until 1999, when the Alpha space station would become the world's primary vehicle for long-term space endurance. The Mir has been manned continuously since September 1989.
The Monday launch went ahead despite questions about the safety of the Soyuz-U booster rocket raised in a front-page article in Friday editions of Izvestia.

Russia's Defense Ministry has banned the use such rockets after a Soyuz-U carrying a military satellite suffered a mechanical failure seconds before lift off in January, said Ivan Safronov, a spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces.

The decision to launch the Soyuz-U rocket and Soyuz TM-25 spacecraft on Monday was approved only after a government commission met last Friday. Another spokesman for the Military Space Forces on Monday said the risk was "minimal."
